{{Short description|Type of integrable system}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Hitchin integrable system''' is an [[integrable system]] depending on the choice of a complex [[reductive group]] and a [[compact space|compact]] [[Riemann surface]], introduced by [[Nigel Hitchin]] in 1987. It lies on the crossroads of [[algebraic geometry]], the theory of [[Lie algebra]]s and [[integrable system]] theory. It also plays an important role in the [[geometric Langlands correspondence]] over the field of [[complex number]]s through [[two-dimensional conformal field theory|conformal field theory]]. 

A [[genus (mathematics)|genus]] zero analogue of the Hitchin system, the [[Garnier integrable system|Garnier system]], was discovered by René Garnier somewhat earlier as a certain limit of the [[Isomonodromic deformation#Fuchsian systems and Schlesinger's equation|Schlesinger equations]], and Garnier solved his system by defining spectral curves. (The Garnier system is the classical limit of the [[Gaudin model]]. In turn, the Schlesinger equations are the classical limit of the [[Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov equations]]).  

Almost all integrable systems of [[classical mechanics]] can be obtained as particular cases of the Hitchin system or their common generalization defined by Bottacin and Markman in 1994.

==Description==

Using the language of algebraic geometry, the [[phase space]] of the system is a partial [[compactification (mathematics)|compactification]] of the [[cotangent bundle]] to the [[moduli space]] of [[stable principal bundle|stable ''G''-bundle]]s for some [[reductive group]] ''G'', on some compact [[algebraic curve]]. This space is endowed with a [[canonical symplectic form]]. Suppose for simplicity that <math>G = \mathrm{GL}(n, \mathbb{C})</math>, the [[general linear group]]; then the [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]]s can be described as follows: the [[tangent space]] to the moduli space of ''G''-bundles at the bundle ''F'' is 

:<math>H^1(\operatorname{End}(F)),</math>

which by [[Serre duality]] is dual to 

:<math>\Phi \in H^0(\operatorname{End}(F)\otimes K),</math> 

where <math>K</math> is the [[canonical bundle]], so a pair 

:<math>(F,\Phi)</math> 

called a Hitchin pair or [[Higgs bundle]], defines a point in the cotangent bundle. Taking 

:<math> \operatorname{Tr}(\Phi^k),\qquad k=1,\ldots,\operatorname{rank}(G)</math>

one obtains elements in 

:<math>H^0( K^{\otimes k} ),</math>

which is a vector space which does not depend on <math>(F,\Phi)</math>. So taking any basis in these vector spaces we obtain functions ''H<sub>i</sub>'', which are Hitchin's hamiltonians. The construction for general reductive group is similar and uses [[Harish-Chandra isomorphism|invariant polynomial]]s on the [[Lie algebra]] of&nbsp;''G''.

For trivial reasons these functions are algebraically independent, and some calculations show that their number is exactly half of the dimension of the phase space. The nontrivial part is a proof of [[Poisson commutativity]] of these functions. They therefore define an integrable system in the symplectic or [[Liouville–Arnold theorem|Arnol'd–Liouville]] sense.

== Hitchin fibration ==
The '''Hitchin fibration''' is the map from the moduli space of Hitchin pairs to [[characteristic polynomial]]s, a higher genus analogue of the map Garnier used to define the spectral curves.  {{harvs|txt|last=Ngô|year1=2006|year2=2010}} used Hitchin fibrations over [[finite field]]s in his proof of the [[fundamental lemma (Langlands program)|fundamental lemma]]. 

To be more precise, the version of Hitchin fibration that is used by Ngô has source the [[Moduli space#Moduli stacks|moduli stack]] of Hitchin pairs, instead of the moduli space. Let <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> be the Lie algebra of the reductive algebraic group <math>G</math>. We have the adjoint action of <math>G</math> on <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. We can then take the [[Quotient stack|stack quotient]] <math>\mathfrak{g}/G </math> and the [[GIT quotient]] <math>\mathfrak{g}/\!/G</math>, and there is a natural morphism <math>\chi:\mathfrak{g}/G\to \mathfrak{g}/\!/G</math>. There is also the natural scaling action of the multiplicative group <math>\mathbb{G}_m</math> on <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, which descends to the stack and GIT quotients. Furthermore, the morphism <math>\chi</math> is equivariant with respect to the <math>\mathbb{G}_m</math>-actions. Therefore, given any [[line bundle]] <math>L</math> on our curve <math>C</math>, we can [[Torsor (algebraic geometry)#The contracted product|twist]] the morphism <math>\chi</math> by the <math>\mathbb{G}_m</math>-[[Torsor (algebraic geometry)|torsor]], and obtain a morphism <math>\chi_L: (\mathfrak{g}/G)_L\to (\mathfrak{g}/\!/G)_L</math> of stacks over <math>C</math>. Finally, the moduli stack of <math>L</math>-twisted Higgs bundles is recovered as the section stack <math>Higgs=Sect(C,(\mathfrak{g}/G)_L)</math>; the corresponding Hitchin base is recovered as <math>A(C,L):=Sect(C,(\mathfrak{g}/\!/G)_L)</math>, which is represented by a vector space; and the Hitchin morphism at the stack level <math>h:Higgs\to A(C,L)</math> is simply the morphism induced by the morphism <math>\chi_L</math> above. Note that this definition is not relevant to semistability. To obtain the Hitchin fibration mentioned above, we need to take <math>L </math> to be the canonical bundle, restrict to the semistable part of <math>Higgs </math>, and then take the induced morphism on the moduli space. To be even more precise, the version of <math>Higgs </math> that is used by Ngô often has the restriction that <math>\deg(L)\geq 2g</math>, so that it cannot be the canonical bundle. This condition is added to guarantee that the topology of the Hitchin morphism is, [[Perverse sheaf|in a precise sense]], determined by its restriction to the smooth part, see {{Harvard citation|Chaudouard|Laumon|2016}} for the vector bundle case.
